title: On-Time Delivery Metric Critique
scenario: A same-day medication delivery service tracks 'Total On-Time Deliveries' as its primary delivery performance metric.
prompt: The operations team reports 'Total On-Time Deliveries' each week to leadership. Last week was 1,200 on-time deliveries, this week is 1,400. Leadership celebrates the improvement. What is wrong with this metric?
instructions: One short sentence: name the flaw, propose a fix. No formulas required.
expected_themes: volume increase does not mean better performance
reference_answer: Should be normalized. On-Time Delivery Rate (on-time deliveries / total deliveries) is better because volume can increase while performance worsens.

grading_rubric.criterion: Identifies lack of normalization as the flaw
grading_rubric.description: Answer explicitly states the metric is not normalized, is a count instead of a rate, or that total volume hides performance

grading_rubric.criterion: Proposes On-Time Delivery Rate or equivalent rate metric
grading_rubric.description: Answer names a rate metric (on-time deliveries / total deliveries, or on-time %), not another count metric

grading_rubric.criterion: Explains why the rate is better
grading_rubric.description: Answer mentions that volume changes can mask performance changes, or that you need to control for total delivery volume

hints: Think about what happens if total delivery volume changes week-over-week.
A count metric can increase even if performance gets worse. How?
The metric does not account for how many total deliveries were attempted.
common_mistakes: Suggesting a median or percentile metric (the flaw is not about outliers, it's about normalization)
Proposing another count metric like 'Total Deliveries' instead of a rate
Focusing on defining 'on-time' threshold instead of identifying the count-vs-rate issue

_meta.scenario: a same day medication delivery service tracking on-time delivery performance
